title: Sustainability and Carbon Accounting
answer: Emissions data, claims checking, combined reporting, disclosure drafting and carbon credit records.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Collecting Emissions Data
children.blurb: Collecting emissions data covers the gathering of greenhouse gas figures across Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3, from fuel bills and meter readings through to supplier reports and spend records.

children.name: Checking Claims Against the Ledger
children.blurb: Checking claims against the ledger is the practice of testing a stated emissions or sustainability figure against the underlying records that are supposed to support it.

children.name: Combining Financial and Non-Financial Data
children.blurb: Combining financial and non-financial data means bringing together figures from the general ledger, such as spend, revenue and cost, with measures that never appear in it, such as emissions, energy use, headcount, water draw or supplier ratings.

children.name: Drafting Sustainability Disclosures
children.blurb: Drafting sustainability disclosures covers the preparation of climate and environmental reporting that companies publish for regulators, investors and the public.

children.name: Carbon Credit Records
children.blurb: Carbon credit records are the documented trail of a unit of greenhouse gas reduction or removal, from the project that generated it through verification, issuance, transfer and retirement.

sections.body: Sustainability and carbon accounting is the work of measuring, recording and reporting what an organisation emits and what it claims about those emissions. In practice, AI systems are being used to pull activity data out of utility bills, fuel purchases, travel records and supplier invoices, then map those entries onto emissions factors. They are also used to scan public statements and marketing copy against the underlying records, flagging claims that the numbers do not support. The field sits at the join between the ledger and the physical world, because a tonne of carbon is not a transaction until someone records it as one. What AI adds is speed and pattern matching across messy documents, not a new definition of what counts as an emission.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Data collection is the most mature part, and even there the hard problem is scope three, where emissions sit with suppliers and customers rather than inside the reporting entity. Claims checking works well when a claim can be tied to a specific figure, and poorly when the claim is qualitative or forward looking. Combined reporting is genuinely difficult because financial and non-financial data run on different cycles, different units and different assurance standards. Disclosure drafting is assisted rather than automated, since frameworks differ by jurisdiction and the wording carries liability. Carbon credit records remain the weakest area, with persistent questions about double counting, retirement and the difference between a credit issued and a credit that represents a real reduction. Nothing here is settled, and no tool removes the need for human judgement about boundaries and estimates.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with Collecting Emissions Data for the raw inputs and the scope problem, since everything downstream depends on it. Checking Claims Against the Ledger is the natural next stop, because it shows how those inputs are used to test public statements rather than to produce them. Combining Financial and Non-Financial Data addresses the reconciliation layer, where emissions figures have to sit alongside the numbers in the accounts, and it is the page for anyone asking how the two reporting streams meet. Drafting Sustainability Disclosures covers the output end, turning reconciled figures into text that satisfies a framework, and it depends on all three earlier pages. Carbon Credit Records stands slightly apart, covering the instruments bought and retired rather than the emissions produced, and it is the page to read when the question is about offsets rather than footprints.
